about.title: Exponential Functions: Growth and Decay
about.length_note: About 30 minutes fits. The class teaches one idea per step (multiplier, initial value, growth, decay, percent link, two graphs, a rule for b), and each step has one check question. Take the pauses you need; the class can be split after the decay beat and finished another day.

say.text: Welcome. Today you will learn to spot an exponential function, tell growth from decay, and sketch its graph. We will go one small step at a time.
A line adds the same amount each step. An exponential function does something different: it multiplies by the same number each step. That number is the constant multiplier.
Here is an example. A clip has 100 views and doubles every day. Each day, we multiply by 2.

show.text:
Day 0: 100 views
Day 1: 200 views
Day 2: 400 views
Day 3: 800 views

ask.q: Views go 100, 200, 400, 800. What is the constant multiplier?
ask.why: 200 ÷ 100 = 2 and 400 ÷ 200 = 2. Each step multiplies by 2. It does not add the same amount.

say.text: We can write this as a rule: y = a · b^x. The a is the starting amount, b is the multiplier, and x counts the steps.

show.text:
y = a · b^x
a = start, b = multiplier, x = steps

ask.q: In y = 100 · 2^x, which number is the multiplier b?
ask.why: b is the number that gets the exponent. The 100 out front is the start.

say.text: Now the starting amount, called the initial value. At x = 0, the power b^0 is 1. So y = a · 1, which is just a.

ask.q: For y = 5 · 3^x, what is y when x = 0?
ask.why: 3^0 = 1, so y = 5 · 1 = 5. The initial value is the number out front.

say.text: Next, growth. If the multiplier b is bigger than 1, every step makes the amount larger. We call b the growth factor. 1.06 is an example.

ask.why: Only 1.2 is bigger than 1. The other two multipliers are less than 1, so they shrink.

say.text: Now decay. If b is between 0 and 1, each step makes the amount smaller. That is a decay factor. 0.97 is an example.

show.text:
Game item worth $60
Loses value: × 0.8 each year
Year 1: $48
Year 2: $38.40

ask.why: We look at b, not a. A multiplier between 0 and 1 shrinks the amount each step.

say.text: Percents give us a shortcut. Gaining 6% each step means b = 1.06. Losing 3% each step means b = 0.97. You start at 1 (that is 100%), then add or subtract the percent.

ask.q: A phone loses 20% of its value each year. What is b?

say.text: Time to graph. Make a table, plot the points, and join them with a smooth curve. Here is y = 100 · 2^x for the views example.

ask.q: Where does the graph in this chart start, at x = 0?
ask.why: At x = 0 the output is the initial value a. Here a = 100.

say.text: Look at the shape. The growth curve bends upward and gets steeper each step. It is not a straight line.

show.text: A curve that starts at 100, rises slowly at first, then climbs faster and faster, bending upward.

ask.right: It starts at a and curves upward, getting steeper
wrong: A curve that falls toward zero
It goes up by the same amount every step
ask.why: Multiplying makes bigger jumps as the amount gets bigger. The result is a curve that bends upward.

say.text: Now the decay graph, for the $60 game item with b = 0.8. It starts at 60 and falls, quickly at first and then more slowly. Each year keeps 80% of what was left, so it falls by less and less.

ask.right: No, it gets closer and closer but never reaches 0
wrong: Yes, once x is big enough
ask.why: Multiplying a positive number by 0.8 again and again always leaves a positive number. The values only get closer to zero.

say.text: Let's graph one from scratch: y = 3 · 2^x. Do the exponent first, then multiply by 3. Then plot the points and draw a smooth curve.

ask.q: For y = 3 · 2^x, what is y when x = 2?
ask.why: Exponent first: 2^2 = 4. Then 3 · 4 = 12. If you got 36, you multiplied 3 · 2 before using the exponent.

say.text: One rule about b. It must be positive and cannot equal 1. If b = 1, you multiply by 1 each time, and nothing ever changes.

ask.q: What does y = 4 · 1^x do as x grows?
ask.right: It stays at 4, so it is not exponential
ask.why: 1^x is always 1, so y is always 4. That is a flat line. It is not growth or decay.

say.text: Let's gather it up. The number out front is the start. The multiplier b is above 1 for growth, or between 0 and 1 for decay. One last check.

show.text:
a = initial value (x = 0)
b > 1: growth, curve bends up
0 < b < 1: decay, curve falls toward 0

ask.q: For y = 500 · 0.9^x, what is the starting value, and is it growth or decay?
ask.why: The number out front, 500, is the start. The multiplier 0.9 is between 0 and 1, so the amount shrinks.

other_side.claim: In this class we write exponential functions as y = a · b^x, with a plain multiplier b.
other_side.other_view: Many textbooks say most real-world growth and decay is written with the number e as the base. The two forms are equivalent, because any y = a·b^x can be rewritten with e. We use a·b^x first because the multiplier is easier to see and to link to percents. The e form comes later in math.
